rebuttal.value:
We thank you for your thoughtful feedback. We appreciate that you found our work to be of good quality, originality, well-written and easy to follow. Moreover, we are grateful that you appreciate our efforts and regard our benchmark to be interesting. We address your comments and concerns below and will update the paper accordingly.

> Although I appreciate the effort of this interesting dataset, I do believe that this paper's novelty is insufficient for this conference. It seems the challenge for future research is unclear (why is this a significant dataset/benchmark for future researchers to continue working on?). 

> The authors can provide more convincing arguments to verify the importance of the motivation for this work. 

Respectfully, we disagree that paper’s novelty is insufficient. Specifically, our work makes the following contributions and provides the following challenges for future research:

1. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first who curated and published a **multiple-round dataset with clicks of real users.** Moreover, we proposed **a novel click collection methodology** for interactive segmentation (IS) task that addresses mask presentation bias. We argue that our methodology can be used for *future research*, including exploring user inputs in other domains (e.g. medical images) and interaction types (contours, strokes, etc.).

2. We developed a click sampling strategy based on **a novel clickability model**. It samples more realistic clicks than baseline strategies, and even allows estimating real-user click probabilities. *Follow-up works* can use our data to further improve predictions of the clickability model, or to develop device-specific models (PC or mobile).

3. We presented RClicks – **a novel benchmark** that leverages the *clickability model* **to estimate the real-world** **performance of IS methods**. Specifically, we demonstrated that **state-of-the-art IS methods experience performance and robustness issues with realistic user clicks**. Thus, there is a quality gap for real-world applications, which can be eliminated using our findings as a guidance. *Future studies* can leverage our clickability model to train IS methods to make them more accessible, useful, and deliver better user experience in real applications.

> If the click closes to the edge, it could be a misoperation by the users. Likely, the user will not expect the output of this interaction. The user will choose to do the next interaction because the cost is acceptable. Moreover, if the user clicks on the edge intentionally, maybe the intent is to select the smaller region/object.

We must confess that this part of the question wasn’t entirely clear to us. We respond according to our understanding of it.

All users were instructed what object or its part should be annotated. After that, we checked all collected clicks and filtered out clicks that fall outside the target object (see Sec. 3 of the paper for details). Therefore, the **collected clicks should be considered to be done** by users **intentionally** and according to the segmentation target.

Nevertheless, we agree that we could not prevent user misoperation, when the user clicks near the object edge. However, we argue that **all** **collected clicks, including possible misoperations, represent real-user behavior patterns for the various IS tasks**. We will add these statements into the camera-ready version of the paper.

Then, *baseline strategy* samples clicks in *the geometric center* according to the distance transform. However, **our data shows that real users do not click based on the *baseline strategy*.** Specifically, real clicks may be located in various parts of the target area, including areas near the object edges (see Fig. 1, 3 in the paper and Fig. 9, 10, 11 in the supplementary), and the baseline click may not maximize users’ click probability (see Fig. 1 in the paper). 

Finally, according to our results (Sec. 6 in the paper), **the *baseline strategy* underestimates the real-world average annotation time (and therefore annotation costs) from 6% up to 30%**, **since it does not sample clicks in accordance with real-users behavior**. In case of annotating a big dataset, unaccounted costs may be significant and may be unacceptable.

> In Sec. 3.1 and Fig. 2, the description of lines 132-134 is different from the annotation in Fig. 2\.

Thanks for carefully reading the manuscript and reporting the writing issues. We will revise the text, and double-check the mistakes in the camera-ready version.

> In Sec. 3.1, why are different time plans (e.g. 1.5s, 2.5s, 2s) for different modes? Please elaborate on it with the scientific basis.

A number of studies have been conducted on this subject [1](Sec. 4), [2](Sec. E.1.2), [3](Sec. 2), [4](Sec. 3.4), [5](Sec. 4.1). Researchers came to the conclusion that the required time plan formula is the following: 1 sec for the annotator to visually locate an object and 1.5 sec for adding each click, while total reported time to localize and click may vary between 1.87s and 2.5s. Since, we did not have the goal of speeding up the labeling of RClicks, but to collect high-quality data, we increased times as follows: showing an image for 1.5s, different mask displaying modes for 2s (since time is needed to localize and remember the target object) and Text Description mode for 2.5s (since more time is needed to read and understand the text). We will add this reasoning and references to the previous works in the camera-ready version.

[1] Delatolas et al. Learning the What and How of Annotation in Video Object Segmentation. WACV 2024

[2] Ravi et al. Sam 2: Segment anything in images and videos. arXiv:2408.00714

[3] Papadopoulos et al. Training object class detectors from eye tracking data. ECCV 2014

[4] Papadopoulos et al. Training object class detectors with click supervision. CVPR 2017

[5] Bearman et al. What’s the point: Semantic segmentation with point supervision. ECCV 2016

Thank you for considerate feedback. We appreciate that you acknowledged our benchmark to be very meaningful, and characterized the overall paper as detailed, relatively smooth and easy to understand. We address your comments below and will include the responses in the camera-ready.

> It seems not very clear on why these five display modes were chosen, is there any basis for explaining that these five modes are reasonable?

Before starting data collection, we considered various ways to visually present the mask and image to a person. These are all the methods we found reasonable. 

Here is a brief story behind choosing display mode:

1. The most unbiased display mode to instruct a participant is considered to be *Text Description*. Since we don’t show the mask anyhow, we don’t have any bias on it. However, we could not use it to annotate all images because such descriptions can be ambiguous. We also cannot use this method for subsequent rounds because we need to indicate the part of the mask that was not segmented in the previous round.   
2. The next display mode we tried was to show the ground truth black-and-white mask (*Silhouette Mask*). In that case, we simply show the mask as is without any modifications. We collected the first batch of data and noticed that participants tend to click to the geometric center of the object. Therefore, this strategy seemed to be biased. We started to look for the least unbiased one.  
3. To prevent people from selecting the geometric center of the object, we added *Object CutOut* mode. We hypothesize that it is harder to be biased on the geometric form of an object when it retains its appearance.  
4. After that, we tried *Shifted CutOut* mode. The idea of this mode was to eliminate dependency on initial cursor position. In that display mode, a person has to move the cursor to the object.  
5. We also tried *Highlighted Instance* mode, since it’s a natural way to highlight an object retaining its' background. We hypothesized that object background may influence click position.

> It’s kind of confusing why not directly use the Text Description mode as the task display mode.

We briefly addressed this in the previous response, but let us provide concrete examples from the TETRIS dataset. Please see figures in the attached PDF.

1. In Fig. 1, there are numerous distinct stones that need to be annotated with the **first click**. Referring to a certain stone only using natural language is extremely challenging.  
2. For an example involving the **second click**, please refer to Fig. 2\. Fig. 2a and 2b depict images with False Positive and False Negative segmentation errors accordingly. These error areas don't have a specific shape. Therefore, it’s very challenging to describe its size and location with a common phrase accurately enough to instruct the user where to click.

> How is the generalization ability of the clickability prediction model? Is it possible that it is limited to a specific dataset and cannot generalize to other real-world datasets?

We computed metrics on click samples for different datasets, as in Table 3 for the validation part of TETRIS dataset. See results below in the table. As one can see, click sampling quality on these datasets mostly is slightly worse than on TETRIS, nevertheless we find these results comparable. Therefore, we conclude that the clickability model is not limited to TETRIS dataset and generalizes well to other datasets of common images.

However, datasets from specific domains, e.g. medical, are out of the scope of our work. For these datasets, additional data collection and evaluations should be done.

We will add the table and this conclusion into the camera-ready version. For the examples of generated clicks for the considered datasets, please refer to Figures 9, 10, 11 of the supplementary.

| Dataset     | KS↑  | PL1↓ | WD↓  | NSS↑  | PDE↑    |
|-------------|------|------|------|-------|---------|
| TETRIS (Val) | 0.46 | 0.38 | 0.08 | 9.08  | 4.64E-05 |
| GrabCut     | 0.39 | 0.41 | 0.10 | 5.63  | 2.12E-04 |
| Berkeley    | 0.43 | 0.39 | 0.09 | 7.29  | 4.99E-04 |
| DAVIS       | 0.42 | 0.41 | 0.10 | 8.55  | 2.53E-04 |
| COCO-MVal   | 0.44 | 0.61 | 0.14 | 10.44 | 7.29E-04 |

rebuttal.value:
We are grateful for your thorough review. We appreciate that you found our study highly meaningful for human-computer interaction research. Specifically, we are encouraged by your assessment of our dataset as a valuable resource for understanding real-world click patterns, and that you appreciated our interactive segmentation benchmark. We address your comments below and will incorporate the feedback in the paper.

> Explain the complexity of the Clickability Model: While the *clickability model* is innovative, its complexity might pose challenges for replication and practical application in different contexts without extensive computational resources. If there is a demonstration of the model’s inference speed and resource usage, it would be even better.

We provide train and inference code, data and weights to replicate the model. Additional information about model architecture and training setup can be found in supplementary A.1. 

We measured inference speed and resource usage of the state-of-the-art segmentation methods and our *clickability model*. All evaluations were done on a single A100. See results in the table below.

| Model               | Params, M | GFLOPs | Mem, Gb | Inference, ms | Input size  |
|---------------------|-----------|--------|---------|---------------|-------------|
| RITM HRNet-32        | 31.95     | 83     | 0.217   | 42 ± 2.0      | 400 × 400   |
| SimpleClick-ViT-H    | 659.39    | 1461   | 2.785   | 41 ± 2.3      | 448 × 448   |
| SAM-ViT-H            | 641.09    | 5473   | 5.745   | 150 ± 2.7     | 1024 × 1024 |
| Clickability model   | 27.59     | 64     | 0.378   | 23 ± 0.9      | 416 × 416   |


As one can see, the *clickability model* is about 2 times faster than RITM and SimpleClick and about 5 times faster than SAM. It also uses a small or a comparable amount of GPU memory.  Note that our model can easily fit on a consumer GPU with 8GB of VRAM. During evaluation on every interaction round, we have to make a single inference of the *clickability model*. Therefore, inference times of *clickability model* and evaluated model are summed up. We found that additional costs from our model are lower or comparable with existing state-of-the-art interactive segmentation methods.

> The data collection includes both PCs and mobile devices. It would be beneficial to explore whether there are differences in clicking behavior across different devices, such as the difference between mouse clicks, touchscreen taps, or swipe gestures

> Exploring the model’s generalization capabilities, such as its performance with gesture operations and other interaction methods.

We examined the differences between PC and mobile device interactions in Sec. B.2 of the supplementary. According to the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (KS), for more than 60% of the compared instances, there were no significant differences between the distributions of clicks on PCs and mobile devices. For illustrations of PC and mobile multi-round clicks, please refer to the attached rebuttal PDF. We will include these illustrations into the camera-ready version of the paper.

In our study, we train a single model across all devices’ clicks to ensure its generality. However, we acknowledge that exploring user behavior on different devices is a direction for future research.

Swipe gestures and other types of user input are outside the scope of the current work. That is because the majority of interactive segmentation models are click-based. Investigating gestures and other types of user interactions is a fruitful area for future exploration.

title.value: RClicks: Realistic Click Simulation for Benchmarking Interactive Segmentation

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper aims to enhances comprehension of real-users actions and facilitate the development of interactive methods by collecting and analyzing 475,000 real-user clicks through a large-scale crowdsourcing study.  The authors developed a clickability model to simulate realistic user clicks and introduced the RClicks benchmark to evaluate the performance and robustness of existing interactive segmentation methods.

review.value:
Strength:
1.  The authors curated a substantial dataset of multiple-round interactions in interactive segmentation, involving diverse user inputs from both PCs and mobile devices. This dataset provides a rich resource for understanding real-world click patterns.
2. The RClicks benchmark offers a way to assess the real-world performance of interactive segmentation methods. By comparing baseline strategy clicks with those generated by the clickability model, the authors provide a more accurate measure of method robustness and effectiveness.
3. The paper conducts thorough evaluations of state-of-the-art methods, revealing that traditional benchmarks may overestimate real-world performance.  Using collected real-user clicks, the paper evaluates the segmentation methods’ performance, offering a grounded assessment of real-world usability.
4. The study’s focus on understanding user click patterns in interactive segmentation tasks is highly meaningful for human-computer interaction research. Given the rapid development of AR/VR technologies, comprehending simple click operations is crucial for enhancing user experience.

Weakness:
1. Explain the complexity of the Clickability Model: While the clickability model is innovative, its complexity might pose challenges for replication and practical application in different contexts without extensive computational resources. If there is a demonstration of the model’s inference speed and resource usage, it would be even better.
2. The data collection includes both PCs and mobile devices. It would be beneficial to explore whether there are differences in clicking behavior across different devices, such as the difference between mouse clicks, touchscreen taps, or swipe gestures

title.value: Review for "RClicks: Realistic Click Simulation for Benchmarking Interactive Segmentation"

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper conducted a crowdsourcing study of click patterns in an interactive segmentation scenario and collected 475K real-user clicks. It also proposed the RClicks benchmark for comprehensively comparing interactive segmentation methods on realistic clicks.

review.value: The quality and originality of this work are good, which clearly clarifies the authors' intention. But there are some doubts about its significance.

strengths.value:
1. It is an interesting idea to sample clicks to propose an RClicks benchmark for assisting interactive segmentation to achieve better performance. I personally appreciate the effort put into collecting this interesting topic.
2. The paper is overall well-written and easy to follow.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. Although I appreciate the effort of this interesting dataset, I do believe that this paper's novelty is insufficient for this conference. It seems the challenge for future research is unclear (why is this a significant dataset/benchmark for future researchers to continue working on?). If the click closes to the edge, it could be a misoperation by the users. Likely, the user will not expect the output of this interaction. The user will choose to do the next interaction because the cost is acceptable. Moreover, if the user clicks on the edge intentionally, maybe the intent is to select the smaller region/object.
2. In Sec. 3.1 and Fig. 2, the description of lines 132-134 is different from the annotation in Fig. 2.
3. In Sec. 3.1, why are different time plans (e.g. 1.5s, 2.5s, 2s) for different modes? Please elaborate on it with the scientific basis.

limitations.value: Please see the Opportunities For Improvement.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value: The authors can provide more convincing arguments to verify the importance of the motivation for this work.

title.value: RClicks: Realistic Click Simulation for Benchmarking Interactive Segmentation

TLDR.value: We benchmark interactive segmentation methods with realistic clicks to obtain quality and robustness metrics that are better aligned with real-world use cases

abstract.value: The emergence of Segment Anything (SAM) sparked research interest in the field of interactive segmentation, especially in the context of image editing tasks and speeding up data annotation. Unlike common semantic segmentation, interactive segmentation methods allow users to directly influence their output through prompts (e.g. clicks). However, click patterns in real-world interactive segmentation scenarios remain largely unexplored. Most methods rely on the assumption that users would click in the center of the largest erroneous area. Nevertheless, recent studies show that this is not always the case. Thus, methods may have poor performance in real-world deployment despite high metrics in a baseline benchmark. To accurately simulate real-user clicks, we conducted a large crowdsourcing study of click patterns in an interactive segmentation scenario and collected 475K real-user clicks. Drawing on ideas from saliency tasks, we develop a clickability model that enables sampling clicks, which closely resemble actual user inputs. Using our model and dataset, we propose RClicks benchmark for a comprehensive comparison of existing interactive segmentation methods on realistic clicks. Specifically, we evaluate not only the average quality of methods, but also the robustness w.r.t. click patterns. According to our benchmark, in real-world usage interactive segmentation models may perform worse than it has been reported in the baseline benchmark, and most of the methods are not robust. We believe that RClicks is a significant step towards creating interactive segmentation methods that provide the best user experience in real-world cases.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
